concepts.title: What is Living: Defining Properties of Life
concepts.definition: Living beings show defining properties such as growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and consciousness, and the ability to respond to the environment, which distinguish them from non-living matter.
concepts.key_idea: Growth by increase in number of cells and self-consciousness are unique to organisms, while metabolism in toto is the surest defining feature of life.
question_patterns: what are the defining properties of living organisms
why is metabolism regarded as a defining property of life
distinguish growth in living beings from growth in non-living objects
why is reproduction not a perfect defining property
how do organisms respond to environmental stimuli
define consciousness as a property of living beings

solution_steps.explain: Check growth, reproduction, metabolism, organisation and response to stimuli in turn.
Mark metabolism and consciousness as defining; note exceptions in reproduction such as sterile workers.
State the set of properties that together mark an object as living.

concepts.title: Biodiversity: Number and Range of Species
concepts.definition: The earth holds enormous biodiversity, with roughly 1.7 to 1.8 million species described and named so far, ranging from microscopic bacteria to giant whales, and their number far exceeds what local experience suggests.
concepts.key_idea: Different regions differ in the number and range of species, which makes identification, nomenclature and classification essential before any biological study.
question_patterns: what is biodiversity and how many species are described so far
why is the number of organisms so large
how do the number and range of species vary from region to region
why is the study of each organism impossible without identification
define biodiversity with examples
why do we need to name and classify organisms

solution_steps.explain: Recall the described number of species and their range of forms.
Contrast the species known locally with the global count.

solution_steps.action: link to the need for taxonomy
solution_steps.explain: Conclude why naming and classification follow from diversity.

concepts.title: Nomenclature and Binomial Nomenclature
concepts.definition: Scientific naming follows the binomial convention given by Carolus Linnaeus, where each organism gets a two-word name of generic and specific epithet written in italics with the generic name capitalised, guided by ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals.
concepts.key_idea: A single scientific name is universal, removing the confusion created by many local names for the same organism.
question_patterns: explain binomial nomenclature with an example
who proposed the binomial system of nomenclature
what are the rules of scientific naming
why are scientific names written in italics
what do ICBN and ICZN stand for
how do local names differ from scientific names

solution_steps.explain: Split the scientific name into genus and species components.
Confirm italics and capitalisation of the generic name.
Name ICBN or ICZN as the guiding code.

concepts.title: Taxonomic Categories: Hierarchy of Classification
concepts.definition: Classification arranges organisms in a taxonomic hierarchy of categories from species and genus through family, order, class, phylum to kingdom, where each higher category includes more general characters and more organisms.
concepts.key_idea: Species is the lowest and basic taxonomic category, and the hierarchy moves from specific characters at the bottom to general characters at the top.
question_patterns: define taxon and taxonomic hierarchy
arrange the taxonomic categories from species to kingdom
why is species the basic unit of classification
how does a genus differ from a family
which category includes organisms of the most general characters
define order and class with examples

solution_steps.explain: Arrange species, genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom in ascending order.
Check that generality of characters increases upwards.
Place a familiar organism such as man or mango in the full hierarchy.

concepts.title: Taxonomical Aids: Herbarium, Museum, Botanical Garden, Key
concepts.definition: Taxonomical aids such as herbarium, botanical garden, museum, zoological park, key, flora, catalogue and monograph store and organise information about diversity, and a key uses paired contrasting statements called couplet and lead to identify organisms.
concepts.key_idea: Keys, floras and monographs make identification possible even where specimens are absent, while herbaria and gardens preserve reference material.
question_patterns: what is a herbarium and how is a specimen preserved in it

solution_steps.action: match the aid to its function
solution_steps.explain: Pair each aid with what it stores or achieves.
Note the couplet and its two leads leading to identification.
